title: The safety system and races
sub: What the Editor catches, why a build stays silent, and what the opt-out attributes cost
cards/0/title: The safety system: who touches what
cards/0/body:
In the Editor every Native container carries a hidden safety handle, an AtomicSafetyHandle. The field exists only under the ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS define, which the Editor has.

On Schedule() the job system records which job reads and which job writes which containers — from the struct’s fields and the [ReadOnly] / [WriteOnly] attributes. Every later schedule and every main-thread access to a container is checked against those marks. Complete() clears them.

The key point: the check does not catch a race as it happens, it checks whether a race is possible from the declarations. So the error shows up on the very first run, even if on your machine the threads would never have collided.
cards/1/title: What gets caught, and with what
cards/1/body:
The four situations interviewers ask about most:

  1. Two independent jobs touch one container and at least one of them writes: InvalidOperationException on the second Schedule(). The message even names the cure — make the first job a dependency of the second. Two readers with [ReadOnly] do not get in each other’s way.
  2. The main thread touches data of a pending job. You may not read while a job that writes the container is unfinished. You may not write while any job that reads or writes it is unfinished. Also an InvalidOperationException.
  3. A write to a [ReadOnly] container inside a job — InvalidOperationException.
  4. An IJobParallelFor writes outside its own range of iterations — IndexOutOfRangeException. The rule is simple: in a parallel job, write only to element [i].
cards/2/q: Which line throws in the Editor?
cards/2/explain: MoveJob writes pos and is not finished yet — Complete() comes only in LateUpdate. The main thread writes to the same container, and the safety system throws an InvalidOperationException. Move the write before Schedule or after Complete().
cards/3/q: MoveJob writes pos. CenterJob only reads pos and marks it [ReadOnly]. Both are scheduled with no dependency. What happens in the Editor?
cards/3/options/0: An InvalidOperationException when CenterJob is scheduled: a reader was scheduled while a writer is unfinished
cards/3/options/3: An exception only in a build
cards/3/explain: [ReadOnly] lets readers run in parallel with each other. A reader next to an unfinished writer is a race: CenterJob may read half-updated positions. The cure is a dependency: schedule CenterJob with MoveJob’s handle.
cards/3/wrong/1: In parallel only with other readers. If someone writes, the reader needs a dependency on it.
cards/3/wrong/2: The job system does not add dependencies by itself — it throws and tells you which one to add.
cards/3/wrong/3: A build has no checks at all: there you get a silent race, not an exception.
cards/4/body:
Safety system checks are unavailable in a build, not “off by default”: their code exists only under ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS, and it does not make it into a standalone player — a Development Build (the one with the profiler and debugging) included. No safety handle, nothing to check against.

The same racy code in a build simply runs: one job reads the positions while another has rewritten half of them. The result is silent data corruption: jittering units, the odd NaN, bugs that show up once in a hundred runs and depend on the device’s core count.

Exceptions in Burst code come with the same warning: in the Editor a throw is caught and logged to the console, but in a build it aborts the application. Mark your own checks [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")] so they leave the build together with Unity’s.

The takeaway: every safety system exception in the Editor is a bug that becomes data corruption in a build. You fix it, you do not silence it.
cards/4/deep: A small subset of checks can be enabled in a player with the UNITY_DOTS_DEBUG define. It is a part of the checks, not the same set as in the Editor, so races are still hunted in the Editor.
cards/5/q: What is true about races and checks in a build? Pick all that apply.
cards/5/options/0: A build has no safety system checks: their code is not compiled into the player
cards/5/options/1: A race in a build means silent data corruption and rare, hard-to-reproduce bugs
cards/5/options/2: A Development Build runs the same checks as the Editor
cards/5/options/3: A throw in Burst code without [Conditional] aborts the application in a build
cards/5/options/4: If the Editor never threw a single exception, the code has no races
cards/5/explain: The checks exist only under ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS and do not reach the player — a Development Build is no exception. A throw in Burst code is an abort in a build. And the absence of exceptions only speaks for the code paths that actually ran in the Editor with checks on.
cards/6/body:
Two different switches, often confused:

  • Edit > Preferences > Jobs > Enable Jobs Debugger — the job system checks: conflicts between jobs and with the main thread. From code, JobsUtility.JobDebuggerEnabled, which only has an effect in the Editor.
  • Jobs > Burst > Enable Safety Checks — Off / On / Force On — the checks inside Burst code (out-of-bounds access, writes to [ReadOnly], the parallel job’s range). It always goes back to On after an Editor reload.

For a single job there is [BurstCompile(DisableSafetyChecks = true)]; Force On overrides that too.

Checks are extra code on every container access. That is why performance is measured in a build, not in the Editor with checks on. And turning checks off to “make the exception go away” means hiding a race.
cards/7/title: Opt-out attributes and what they cost
cards/7/body:
Sometimes the safety system is too strict for correct code. That is what these attributes are for:

  • [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction] — a parallel job may write to other indices. Used for scatter writes when there is no overlap by construction.
  • [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction] — no checks at all for this field.
  • [NativeDisableUnsafePtrRestriction] — allows a pointer field in a job.

The cost: an attribute does not make code safe, it removes the net and puts the proof on you. A race stops being an exception in the Editor and becomes silent everywhere. And Burst treats fields with [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction] as possibly aliasing, which may cost optimizations.

The order: first a dependency, [ReadOnly] or splitting the data; an attribute only with a comment explaining why there is no race.
cards/8/q: Match each situation with what happens or what you need
cards/8/pairs/0/0: An IJobParallelFor writes to an element outside its range
cards/8/pairs/1/0: Two independent jobs write to one array
cards/8/pairs/2/0: The same race in a build
cards/8/pairs/3/0: You must write to other indices, with no overlap by construction
cards/9/title: Fix it with a dependency, not an opt-out
cards/9/body:
The exception message tells you what to do: pass the previously scheduled job as a dependency of the new one. The last parameter of Schedule is JobHandle dependsOn: the new job will not start until the dependency has finished. The safety system sees the order and stays quiet.

The main thread does not wait here — unlike Complete() between jobs. The worker threads wait, and only for each other.

Other honest fixes: merge the two steps into one job, or give each job its own container (a double buffer). How to build a whole frame’s graph out of dependencies is the next lesson.
cards/10/task: In Swarm, CenterJob reads pos while MoveJob writes it, and in the Editor Schedule throws. Fix it with a dependency: pass MoveJob’s handle to avg.Schedule and mark pos in CenterJob [ReadOnly]. Keep Complete() in LateUpdate and do not use opt-out attributes.
cards/10/checks/0/label: CenterJob is scheduled with a dependency on MoveJob’s handle
cards/10/checks/1/label: In CenterJob the pos field is marked [ReadOnly]
cards/10/checks/4/label: In LateUpdate Complete() comes before reading center.Value
cards/10/explain: With the dependency CenterJob starts only after MoveJob, and completing the single last handle in LateUpdate completes both. [ReadOnly] is not required by the safety system here, but it describes the access honestly and lets other readers of pos run in parallel with CenterJob. In an interview: “a safety system exception is a race; I fix it with a dependency, not by turning the checks off.”
cards/11/q: Interviewer: “In the Editor everything is clean, but in an Android build units sometimes jitter. The positions job has [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction].” What do you suspect first?
cards/11/options/0: A race: the attribute hid it in the Editor, and a build has no checks at all — one job reads the positions while another writes them
cards/11/options/2: A batchSize that is too small
cards/11/explain: A classic: the check was disabled because “the exception was in the way”. The Editor went quiet, the build never had checks, and the phone’s core count and timings differ — so the race surfaced. Remove the attribute, look at the exception in the Editor and fix it with a dependency.
cards/11/wrong/1: Float differences do happen, but an opt-out attribute on the positions container is a far likelier cause.
cards/11/wrong/2: batchSize affects speed, not data correctness.
cards/11/wrong/3: Blaming the compiler is the last resort when the code has race checks turned off.
